title: Play to Your Strengths
hook: Fourteen capabilities in the review, three required by the strategy. The other eleven were why the three never built actual advantage.
counterintuition: Most organizations find they have more capabilities than their strategy needs. That abundance is the warning sign. A capability that does not connect to the how-to-win choice consumes investment without compounding toward any advantage.
tryThisNow: State your current how-to-win choice in one sentence. Then name the three specific things your organization must be able to do well for that choice to work. For each one, rate honestly: have it, building it, or not yet exists. The gap is where the investment belongs: not at the top of a strengths list.
keyTakeaway: The capability audit runs backward from the how-to-win choice: what must the strategy require, not what the organization currently does well.

breakdown.fastRead:
Leon ran a landscape architecture firm with genuine skill in four areas: ecological restoration, residential garden design, commercial plaza work, and public park planning. Each area was real. His business development presentation listed all four.

He landed no significant work for six months.

When he traced where the firm's strongest projects had come from, the answer was specific: complex ecological restoration for land trusts and conservation organizations. Those clients needed scientific knowledge, community engagement, and regulatory navigation that most design firms could not provide together. The other three areas were solid. They were not the system that made the firm irreplaceable.

Leon was not weak in the other three areas. He was diluting the one area that made the firm irreplaceable.

He rebuilt the presentation around the capability system the ecological work required. The next three pitches were won against firms that offered broader services.
breakdown.deepRead:
A capability system is the set of specific things an organization must be able to do well for its how-to-win choice to deliver a genuine advantage. It is not a list of what the organization currently does. It is what the strategy requires.

The distinction matters because the how-to-win choice sets the direction first. The capability audit runs backward from it. The question is not which strengths are impressive or historically significant; the question is which capabilities are required to deliver the advantage the strategy has chosen to build.

Gillette fit because the things Gillette was able to do well were the specific things P&G's strategy needed done. Precision manufacturing, deep consumer insight, and global distribution capabilities reinforced P&G's how-to-win choices in a specific set of consumer categories. The acquisition was not justified by Gillette's market position or brand value alone; it was justified by capability fit. What Gillette could do well was what P&G's strategy required to be done well.

An isolated strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice is not a strategic advantage. It is a cost. The organization must invest to maintain it, and the investment does not compound toward the advantage the strategy is trying to build.

The backward-mapping question is: what would the organization need to be able to do, specifically and at a high level, for the how-to-win choice to work? The answer defines the required capability system. Checking honestly whether that system exists, is under construction, or has not yet been started is the capability audit that matters.
breakdown.fullRead:
Most capability conversations start from what the organization already has: a list of things it does well, accumulated over time, organized by department or function. The question is then how to use those strengths to build strategy. But that sequence produces a strategy shaped by what exists, not a capability system built for what the strategy requires.

Starting from the how-to-win choice runs in the opposite direction. The question is not what can we do with what we have, but what must we be able to do well for this specific advantage to work in this specific field? That question produces a different answer, and the answer often includes capabilities the organization does not yet have.

What makes a capability system different from a list of strengths is that the required capabilities reinforce each other. A strength that operates in isolation is useful but not compounding. A capability system is a set of activities where each one makes the others more effective. A firm that builds deep industry knowledge develops the regulatory familiarity that accelerates client trust, which generates the referral network that brings in the next case, which adds another layer of industry pattern-recognition. The activities support each other. Remove any one, and the others work less well. That is the difference between a list and a system.

Gillette illustrated what capability fit looks like when the backward mapping is done right. P&G did not acquire Gillette because the brand was large or the market position was strong. P&G acquired Gillette because Gillette's capability system reinforced what P&G's strategy needed done. The fit was in the activities, not in the revenue size or brand recognition, which were real but secondary to the strategic question.

An isolated strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice creates cost, not advantage. The organization must fund it, staff it, and maintain it, and none of that investment compounds toward the advantage the cascade is trying to build.

Now apply the backward-mapping question to your own situation. Name your current how-to-win choice. Then list the three things your organization would need to do exceptionally well for that choice to produce a genuine advantage in the field you have chosen. Check each one honestly: does the capability exist at the required level, is it under construction, or does it not yet exist? The gap between what the strategy requires and what the capability system can currently deliver is where the investment question belongs.

The capability audit is not a performance review. It is a strategic question: does the activity system we currently have point in the direction the how-to-win choice requires? If it does not, the gap is a strategic decision, not an operational one. Naming it clearly is the first step toward addressing it deliberately.

examples.title: Emily Asks Which Clients Actually Choose Them for the Design

planSpec.domain: an architecture studio evaluating a partnership with a construction management firm
planSpec.audience: a studio principal deciding whether to absorb a construction management team to offer design-build services
planSpec.stakes: construction management requires an activity system that is fundamentally different from the studio's design capabilities
planSpec.requiredBeat: Emily asks which clients choose them for design versus build management and realizes the studio's activity system is built entirely around the former

examples.scenario: 'We can offer clients everything under one roof.' Emily's potential partner described the design-build opportunity over the phone: her studio would handle design, his construction management firm would handle the build. A term sheet was on her desk. Before agreeing, she asked him a question: which of her clients in the past three years had chosen the studio specifically for the design, and which had asked about construction management? The answer was immediate and one-sided. Every client in her file had hired a separate construction manager. Not one had come to her for both. The two client types were different people who valued different things. Her studio's activity system was built entirely around the former.
examples.whatToDo: Map the activities the design-build partnership would require: scheduling systems, site supervision culture, construction contract management. Check each against the studio's current activity system. The overlap reveals whether the capability fit is real or assumed before any term sheet is signed.
examples.whyItMatters: A design-build partnership adds a capability system the studio does not currently have. Building it requires adding scheduling, supervision, and contract expertise while maintaining the design capability the existing clients are paying for. Activity system mismatch shows up as diluted quality in both directions.

examples.title: Ryan's Board Checks the Capability Before the Budget

planSpec.domain: a rural hospital evaluating whether to add an oncology unit
planSpec.audience: a hospital administrator responding to community demand for local cancer care
planSpec.stakes: an oncology unit requires a capability system the hospital's primary and emergency care infrastructure was not built to support
planSpec.requiredBeat: a retired oncologist board member asks Ryan to check five required activities against the hospital's current capability, and by the third check the room understands the gap is a decade-long build

examples.scenario: At 9:00, Ryan presents the oncology unit proposal to the board. Two slides: rising cancer diagnosis rates in the county, forty minutes of travel time to the nearest oncology center. The case for the unit is obvious. A board member who is also a retired oncologist raises her hand and asks: can you list the five activities the unit would need to perform consistently to deliver safe oncology care? Ryan lists them: specialized oncology nurses, a radiation therapy facility, oncology pharmacy capability, a radiologist with oncology certification, and patient volume high enough to sustain specialist salaries. She then asks him to check each one against the hospital's current capability. By the third check, the room understands the gap is not a funding question. It is a decade-long capability build.
examples.whatToDo: Before the capability funding request, list the five most critical activities the new unit would require at a consistent quality level. Check each one against the current activity system. The ones not present are not budget items; they are the activity system the strategy would need to build before the unit can open safely.
examples.whyItMatters: Community demand for a service is not the same as a capability to deliver it. The question for the hospital board is not whether cancer patients need care locally but whether the activity system required to provide that care safely can be built at this hospital's scale without compromising the existing capability.

examples.title: Antoine's Online Cohort Shows What Did Not Transfer

planSpec.domain: a coding bootcamp deciding whether to add a part-time online program alongside its full-time in-person curriculum
planSpec.audience: a program director reviewing the results of an online pilot cohort
planSpec.stakes: the activity system driving in-person outcomes does not translate to the online format without being rebuilt from scratch
planSpec.requiredBeat: six months of online cohort data reveals that the activity system producing in-person placements did not transfer

examples.scenario: Six months after launching the online pilot, Antoine reviewed the graduation and placement numbers. Completion rate for the online cohort: forty-four percent. For the in-person program: eighty-eight percent. Employer partnership calls for the online cohort: three. For the in-person program in the same period: eleven. He had assumed the curriculum would work across both formats. The placement data said something different. The in-person program's results were driven by cohort accountability, joint debugging sessions, and a pair-programming culture that formed through daily proximity. Online, those interactions were optional. Employer calls had dropped because hiring managers had noticed that online graduates arrived without the collaborative habits the in-person graduates had built. The activity system that produced placement outcomes did not transfer.
examples.whatToDo: Before launching the next online cohort, name the three activity-system elements responsible for the in-person placement rate. For each one, design a specific equivalent the online format can actually deliver. If none of those equivalents are feasible within the online model, the online cohort is a different product that requires a different capability system built from the start.
examples.whyItMatters: A program format that looks the same on a course outline requires a completely different activity system when the delivery medium changes. Completion and placement outcomes are the evidence that the capability system either translated or did not.

examples.title: Catarina's Warehouse Gets the Product to the Shelf. It Stops There.

planSpec.domain: a specialty food distributor considering moving into direct retail sales
planSpec.audience: a distribution company owner who has signed a retail supply agreement with a major retailer
planSpec.stakes: distribution logistics and retail brand capability are two different activity systems that share a supply chain but require completely different organizational capabilities
planSpec.requiredBeat: the first retail season reveals that logistics skill has no capability in the consumer brand decisions that move product from shelf to basket

examples.scenario: The warehouse smelled of cardboard and cold storage, optimized for movement: pallets in, pallets out, routes planned to minimize truck idle time. Before: Catarina signed the retail supply agreement after a meeting where the margin projection looked strong. Her team was exceptional at distribution logistics: route planning, supplier relationships, cold chain management, and inventory turnover. After: the first season's sell-through data arrived. The product had moved from warehouse to shelf. It had not moved from shelf to basket. The retail buyer called to discuss promotional strategy. Catarina's team had no one who knew how to design a retail promotion, negotiate endcap placement, or build the packaging story that drives a consumer to pick up an unfamiliar product. The activity systems were completely different.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next retail supply agreement, list the activities required to move product from shelf to basket: promotional planning, endcap negotiation, consumer packaging decisions, retail buyer relationship management. Check whether any of these currently exist in the organization. The ones that do not are not services to hire; they are an activity system to build.
examples.whyItMatters: Distribution logistics and retail brand management are two activity systems that share a supply chain but require completely different organizational capabilities. Entering retail distribution without the second system in place produces a shelf presence that does not convert.

examples.title: Pavel Imagines What the Partner Curator Would Need and Finds the Gap

planSpec.domain: a museum evaluating whether to build a traveling exhibition capability
planSpec.audience: a curator whose museum has a strong permanent collection but is being asked by a donor to develop touring exhibitions
planSpec.stakes: a traveling exhibition capability requires a different activity system than a permanent collection, and building it draws from the curatorial staff's research capacity
planSpec.requiredBeat: Pavel imagines the first traveling show at a partner museum and realizes the operational precision required is not in the current activity system and training for it pulls from the research function

examples.scenario: You are running the thought experiment with Pavel. The donor proposal is for three touring exhibitions over five years. He imagines the first show arriving at a partner museum: the partner curator sends installation requirements three weeks out. The crates travel with a specialist conservator. The lighting specs require an electrician familiar with museum climate standards. The installation schedule requires a site supervisor who can adapt to a different building's constraints on the fly. Pavel's curatorial staff is exceptional at scholarly interpretation and permanent collection research. None of them had been asked to coordinate a multi-city installation logistics system. He asks his deputy: how long would it take to build the operational capability the touring program requires without pulling the curatorial team away from the research work that makes this museum worth visiting? The answer makes the donor proposal look different.
examples.whatToDo: Before accepting the touring exhibition proposal, list the activities a traveling show requires that the permanent collection model does not: logistics coordination, partner museum relations, on-site installation management, specialized conservation transport. Calculate the resource cost of building those capabilities against the cost of diverting curatorial staff from the research function. Name the trade-off explicitly before accepting.
examples.whyItMatters: A traveling exhibition capability requires an activity system built around operational flexibility and logistics precision. A permanent collection capability requires an activity system built around scholarly depth and interpretive quality. Building both simultaneously pulls the activity systems in opposite directions.

examples.title: Ingrid Reviews Two Years of Capability Mismatch

planSpec.domain: a sailing club considering whether to add a competitive racing program to its recreational sailing membership
planSpec.audience: a club commodore whose facilities were designed for recreational adult sailors
planSpec.stakes: a competitive racing program requires an activity system that conflicts with the recreational club's existing facility allocation and coaching model
planSpec.requiredBeat: two years of racing program data reveals that the capability fit was never established before the program launched, and the club's existing activity system reliably undermined it

examples.scenario: Two years after launching the racing program, Ingrid reviewed the membership data. The coaching hire had left after fourteen months: the club's slip assignments prioritized recreational members by seniority, which created regular availability conflicts for the racing fleet. Of the twenty-four competitive members who joined in the first year, eighteen had departed. Their resignation notes cited the same two issues: coaching inconsistency and facility conflicts. The recreational membership had grown. The racing program had collapsed. The capability fit problem had been visible before the launch if anyone had listed the five activities a competitive racing program required and checked them against the club's facility configuration, slip allocation system, and coaching hire model.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next program expansion, list the five activity-system requirements the new program cannot run without: dedicated slip allocation, coaching credentials and schedule continuity, racing-specific equipment maintenance, a competition calendar that does not conflict with recreational booking. Check each against what the club currently has. The ones missing are conditions that must exist before the program is viable, not items to address after the launch.
examples.whyItMatters: A recreational sailing club and a competitive racing program are two activity systems housed in the same facility. Adding the second without building the activity system it requires produces a program that the facility's existing configuration will reliably undermine.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a strategy-specific capability system from a general list of organizational strengths?
choices: A capability system includes only capabilities the organization is currently investing to build; a strength list includes historical capabilities.
A capability system is defined by working backward from the how-to-win choice to identify specific required activities; a strength list is assembled from what the organization currently does well.
A capability system is a ranked list of the organization's top strengths sorted by relevance to current market conditions.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is the direction of the analysis. A strength list starts from what exists. A capability system starts from what the strategy requires and works backward. Strengths that do not connect to the how-to-win choice are costs, not advantages, regardless of how well-developed they are.

questions.prompt: A software company's how-to-win choice is to be the most reliable platform for financial services teams that cannot afford system downtime. Which backward-mapping question best identifies the required capability system?
choices: What must the company be able to do consistently well for financial services teams to choose this platform over alternatives when downtime risk is their primary concern?
What features do our financial services customers most frequently request in product reviews?
What is the company's current best technical capability that already differentiates it in the enterprise market?
questions.explanation: The backward-mapping question starts from the how-to-win choice (reliability for downtime-averse financial teams) and asks what activity system must exist to deliver that specific advantage. Feature requests and current differentiators are both useful but describe what exists, not what the strategy requires for this specific field and customer.

questions.prompt: A coding bootcamp's in-person program achieves eighty-eight percent completion and strong employer placement. A new online cohort achieves forty-four percent completion and weaker placement. What does this gap most likely indicate?
choices: Online learners are inherently less motivated than in-person learners and require stronger incentive structures.
The online cohort needs a better candidate screening process to attract more committed applicants.
The in-person activity system (cohort accountability, pair programming, proximity-built habits) did not transfer; the online format needs a different activity system built for it.
questions.explanation: Motivation and screening are not the root cause. The completion and placement data reveal an activity system problem: the in-person program's results depend on activities that the online format cannot replicate without being redesigned. The online cohort needs its own capability system built for its specific format, not a copy of the in-person one.

questions.prompt: A specialty food distributor signs a retail supply agreement. After the first season, sell-through is poor and retail buyers ask about promotional strategy the distributor cannot execute. What does this reveal?
choices: The distributor's activity system was built for logistics, not the consumer brand decisions that move product from shelf to basket; the two systems were never audited against each other before the agreement was signed.
The distributor needs to hire a retail marketing consultant to provide promotional expertise for the current season.
The distributor moved too quickly; a consumer brand division should have been built before approaching retailers.
questions.explanation: A staffing gap or timing error are operational diagnoses. The case reveals an activity system mismatch: distribution logistics and retail brand management require fundamentally different activities. Signing the retail agreement without auditing the capability gap produced a predictable result: a shelf presence the missing consumer brand system could not convert to a purchase.

questions.prompt: P&G's acquisition of Gillette was justified on the basis of capability fit. Which question best represents the backward-mapping logic that made the acquisition compelling?
choices: Is Gillette the largest available acquisition target in a category adjacent to P&G's existing portfolio?
Do Gillette's specific capabilities (precision manufacturing, consumer insight, global distribution) reinforce the activities P&G's how-to-win choices require in their target consumer categories?
Will acquiring Gillette produce the highest revenue synergies available in the current acquisition environment?
questions.explanation: Acquisition size and revenue synergies are financial metrics, not strategic ones. The backward-mapping logic asks whether Gillette's activity system reinforces P&G's required capabilities. Gillette fit because the things Gillette could do well were specifically the things P&G's strategy needed done, not because of market position or brand value alone.

questions.prompt: A rural hospital's administrator lists five activities an oncology unit would require and checks each against the hospital's current capability. Three of the five are absent. What is the most accurate interpretation?
choices: The community demand justifies building the three missing capabilities before the unit opens.
The hospital should partner with a regional cancer center to fill the gaps temporarily.
The audit reveals an activity system the hospital does not have; building it is a strategic decision (not a budget item) that must be made before the unit is approved.
questions.explanation: Community demand does not resolve a capability gap. Temporary partnerships are operational tools, not strategic answers. The backward-mapping audit revealed that the oncology unit requires an activity system the hospital does not have. Building it is a decade-long commitment that must be evaluated as a strategic choice, not as a service addition.

questions.prompt: An architecture studio is considering a design-build partnership. The studio's clients have historically hired separate construction managers. Which action best represents the capability audit?
choices: List the activities construction management requires (scheduling systems, site supervision, contract management) and check each against the studio's current activity system to identify the gap before deciding.
Survey current clients about whether they would prefer a single vendor for design and construction services.
Ask the construction management partner to handle all construction activities so the studio only needs to contribute design.
questions.explanation: Client surveys identify demand, not capability fit. Delegating to the partner avoids the audit entirely. The capability audit must list the activities the partnership requires from the studio's side and check whether those activities exist in the current system. That check determines whether the partnership adds a genuine capability or exposes a gap.

questions.prompt: A sailing club adds a competitive racing program. After two years, the coaching hire has left, the racing fleet is underutilized due to slip conflicts, and competitive members have departed citing coaching inconsistency. What is the correct strategic diagnosis?
choices: The club hired the wrong coach and needs to improve its recruiting process for the next hire.
The racing program needed dedicated slips, coaching continuity, and fleet priority: an activity system the recreational club's setup could not support; no capability audit was done before launch.
The recreational membership's seniority-based slip allocation is unfair to competitive members and should be restructured.
questions.explanation: A hiring error or a policy change are operational diagnoses. The strategic diagnosis is an activity system mismatch: the racing program required a facility configuration and resource allocation that the recreational club's existing system could not accommodate without being restructured. The capability audit should have identified this before the program launched.

questions.prompt: A museum director is evaluating a donor proposal for three touring exhibitions over five years. The museum's permanent collection capability is built around deep scholarly research and interpretive depth. Which evaluation is most strategically sound?
choices: Accept the proposal because donor relationships are strategically important and capability gaps can be addressed as they arise.
Accept one touring exhibition as a pilot and evaluate whether the capability can be built from the experience.

Map the activities a touring show requires against the current system, name the gaps, and decide whether building the touring capability reinforces or dilutes the permanent collection strategy before accepting.
questions.explanation: Accepting for donor relationship reasons or piloting without the capability audit both skip the strategic question. The evaluation must start from the backward-mapping question: what does the touring capability require, and does building it reinforce or draw from the activity system the permanent collection strategy depends on? That answer determines whether the proposal is a strategic fit or a capability distraction.

reviewCards.front: What is a strategy-specific capability system?
reviewCards.back: The specific set of activities the organization must perform at a consistently high level for its how-to-win choice to deliver a genuine advantage. It is defined by working backward from the strategy, not assembled from what the organization currently does well.

reviewCards.front: What backward-mapping question identifies required capabilities?
reviewCards.back: What must the organization be able to do well, specifically and consistently, for the how-to-win choice to work in the chosen field? The answer defines the required capability system and reveals where the gaps are.

reviewCards.front: What made the Gillette acquisition a strategic capability fit for P&G?
reviewCards.back: Gillette's activity system reinforced what P&G's strategy needed done. The fit was in specific capabilities (precision manufacturing, consumer insight, global distribution) that pointed in the same direction as P&G's how-to-win choices, not in Gillette's brand size or market position alone.

reviewCards.front: Name two effects of adding a new offering without auditing the activity system first.
reviewCards.back: The new offering requires capabilities the organization does not have. The gap shows up as diluted performance in the new offering and as resources drawn away from the activity system the existing strategy depends on. Both suffer.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between a strength and a required capability?
reviewCards.back: A strength is something the organization does well. A required capability is something the strategy needs done well to produce advantage in the chosen field. A strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice creates cost, not advantage.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to audit capabilities by working backward from the how-to-win choice, not forward from a list of current strengths. You practice the backward-mapping question and apply it to identify specific capability gaps before committing to a new offering, partnership, or expansion.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a new service or product offering
ifThenPlans.plan: Before committing, list the activities the new offering would require from the organization at a consistently high level. Check each one against the existing activity system. The ones not present are not items to add later; they are capabilities that must be built before the offering can be delivered at the quality the strategy requires.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a proposed acquisition or partnership
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask whether the acquisition or partner's specific capabilities reinforce the activities your how-to-win choice requires. If the activities point in the same direction, the fit is real. If the acquired capabilities require a different activity system, the acquisition is a distraction from the existing strategy.

ifThenPlans.context: allocating development budget across multiple capabilities
ifThenPlans.plan: Start from the how-to-win choice and list the capabilities it requires. Allocate the development budget to those first. Investment in a capability that is not required by the strategy is overhead regardless of how well-developed it is.

ifThenPlans.context: deciding whether to pursue a new customer segment or channel
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask whether serving the new segment requires the same activity system as the current strategy or a different one. A different activity system means a second strategy that must be evaluated on its own terms, not an extension of the first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: State your current how-to-win choice in one sentence. Then name the three specific activities your organization must perform at a high level for that choice to work. For each one, rate honestly: have it, building it, or not yet started. The ones not yet started are the gaps the investment conversation should be about.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: When a new opportunity, request, or partnership comes up, run the backward-mapping question before deciding. Ask what activities the new opportunity requires from your organization and whether those activities reinforce or pull from the current capability system. Name the answer before saying yes.

memorableLines.text: Leon was not weak in the other three areas. He was diluting the one area that made the firm irreplaceable.
memorableLines.why: The two-sentence contrast names the trap precisely: not a weakness problem but a concentration problem, where strength in too many directions prevents advantage in any one.

memorableLines.text: Gillette fit because the things Gillette was able to do well were the specific things P&G's strategy needed done.
memorableLines.why: The sentence compresses the capability-fit concept into the most portable form: not size, not brand, not market position, but activity alignment.

memorableLines.text: An isolated strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice creates cost, not advantage.
memorableLines.why: The one-sentence rule gives the reader a test they can apply to any strength on any list: does it compound toward the strategy, or just maintain itself?
